name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,614

clue.text: Fun was had in bed cavorting as newlyweds?

indicators.note: cavorting is leaping about wildly, so the letters jump out of their order

blocks.note: all fourteen letters of the phrase are the raw material

explanation.surface: A cheeky picture of a honeymoon couple romping in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a joke about the wedding night, and the fodder is the whole first half of the clue, word lengths ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: Newlyweds are a recently married couple, so the pair is a man and his spouse; the question mark flags the loose fit.

clue.text: Keeps nursing old leader of French general legislature

indicators.note: to nurse is to cradle something in your arms, so one piece wraps around the others
the leader is whatever stands at the front, so only the opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: to house something is to keep or shelter it
O is the standard abbreviation for old
the opening letter of the word French
common in the sense of shared by all, widespread

explanation.surface: Someone tending an elderly French general who once led a legislature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeps' looks like the verb running the sentence, but it is the container that wraps everything else, while 'general' is an adjective meaning shared by all.
explanation.definitionFit: The lower chamber of the UK Parliament is the elected body that makes laws, so it is a legislature.

clue.text: Joint that is primarily raunchy and more disreputable

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so just the opening letter is used

blocks.note: a seam is the line where two pieces are joined
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
opening letter of raunchy

explanation.surface: A dodgy nightclub described as mostly raunchy and getting worse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' suggests a seedy bar, which fits the surface, but here it is a sewing join.
explanation.definitionFit: Seamy means sordid and unpleasant, so its comparative describes something of worse repute.

clue.text: Mineral article absorbed by metal kitchen implement

indicators.note: what is absorbed is soaked up and held inside something else

blocks.note: Al is the chemical symbol for aluminium
the indefinite article
a baster is a bulb-and-tube tool for spooning juices over roasting meat

explanation.surface: A piece of rock somehow soaked up by a metal cooking utensil.
explanation.walkthrough: The metal and the kitchen implement are separate pieces, and the article slips between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Alabaster is a fine-grained white form of gypsum used for carving, a naturally occurring mineral.

clue.text: Live with women in small valley

indicators.note: something in a place is enclosed by it

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for women
a dell is a small wooded hollow

explanation.surface: Setting up home with female company in a little valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live with women' reads as one phrase, but 'with' only joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell somewhere is to reside or make your home there, a formal synonym.

clue.text: Careless man from Newcastle holds informal party

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside your grip

blocks.note: NE is the postcode area for Newcastle upon Tyne, in the North East of England
a gent is a gentleman
a lig is British slang for a freeloaders' party or event

explanation.surface: A Geordie who throws a casual party and doesn't care how it goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man from Newcastle' suggests a Geordie, but it is split: the place gives its postcode and the man is a gent, read in reverse order.
explanation.definitionFit: Negligent means failing to take proper care, which is the plain sense of careless.

clue.text: What Shakespeare did with Henry the Fourth or the equivalent

definitions.text: What Shakespeare did with Henry the Fourth or the equivalent

blocks.clueFragment: What Shakespeare did with Henry the Fourth
blocks.note: surface reading: how the playwright treated a king, perhaps flattering him or reshaping history
setter's reading: Henry the Fourth is the play, and the deed is the same one he did for every other play

explanation.walkthrough: Henry the Fourth looks like the monarch, but it is the title of the history play; the deed is simply authorship.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare composed the play Henry IV, so the past tense of the verb for authoring a text describes his act.

clue.text: Dissension following trial

blocks.note: f. is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
a legal action is a lawsuit heard in court

explanation.surface: Quarrels breaking out after a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' reads as 'after', but it is the abbreviation used in page references.
explanation.definitionFit: Faction can mean internal strife or conflict within a group, a less common sense than a breakaway group.

clue.text: Old description of Smilodon!

blocks.note: first meaning: elderly, getting on in years
second meaning, read literally: the sabre-toothed cat had enormous fangs

explanation.walkthrough: Smilodon is the extinct sabre-toothed cat; the idiom for being aged is taken literally for its huge canines, and the exclamation mark flags the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom comes from horses' gums receding with age, and it fits a prehistoric beast with dagger-like fangs.

clue.text: Ignorant article in Le Monde about American conflict

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the outside of the rest

blocks.note: une is a French indefinite article, as would appear in the Paris newspaper
A is a standard abbreviation for American
a war is an armed conflict

explanation.surface: A clueless piece in a French newspaper about a US war.
explanation.walkthrough: Le Monde is a French daily, so its article is a French word, not a news story.
explanation.definitionFit: To be ignorant of something is to lack knowledge of it, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Complain about name-dropping in club

indicators.note: what is dropped is let fall and left out

blocks.note: to grouch is to grumble
on as in a talk on a subject
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Grumbling about people who show off by mentioning famous acquaintances at a members' club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Name-dropping' is a real habit, but here the hyphenated phrase tells you to remove a letter. The Groucho Club is a private members' club in London's Soho popular with media people.
explanation.definitionFit: The Groucho Club is a well-known London private members' club, so its first word stands as a crossword-only sense here.

clue.text: Heather regularly spent years in Chad

indicators.note: letters spent at regular intervals are used up every other one, leaving the rest

blocks.note: the even-placed letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: A woman named Heather living for years in the African country of Chad.
explanation.walkthrough: Heather and Chad both look like people's names, but the first is a plant and the second is just letter material.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is the botanical genus name for heathers, the low shrubs of moorland.

clue.text: Lurking wild lion and tiger

indicators.note: wild means untamed and out of control, so the letters run riot

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Big cats in the wild, hiding and waiting to pounce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' sits naturally beside the animals, which is what hides its role.
explanation.definitionFit: Lurking and hanging about both describe lingering somewhere without obvious purpose, so they are near synonyms.

clue.text: Eve maybe one on board

blocks.note: first meaning: the original wife, partner of Adam in Genesis
second meaning: a ship's officer ranking below the captain

explanation.walkthrough: Eve was Adam's partner and the first woman, so she was the original spouse; 'maybe' flags her as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both the original partner in Eden and the deck officer next in command after a ship's captain.

clue.text: Attending twice today

blocks.note: at as in at a meeting, being there
the same sense again: being present means attending

explanation.surface: Going to two sessions in the same day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twice' tells you to take two different words that each mean attending and join them.
explanation.definitionFit: Today here means nowadays, the current time, which matches the phrase for right now.

clue.text: Charlie meets unknown cleric

blocks.note: Charlie is the NATO alphabet word for C
anon. abbreviates anonymous, author unknown

explanation.surface: A man called Charlie is introduced to a mysterious priest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unknown' tempts the algebraic X or Y, but it is the anonymous byline.
explanation.definitionFit: A canon is a clergyman attached to a cathedral chapter, one kind of churchman.

clue.text: Chemical engineer defends right to telephone customers

indicators.note: to defend is to stand guard around something, protecting it on all sides

blocks.note: the initial letters of the two words, the usual abbreviation for the profession
a lien is a legal right to hold property until a debt is paid
tel. is the usual abbreviation for telephone

explanation.surface: An engineer upholding the right to cold-call customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' suggests R or a direction; here it is the legal claim, and with the phone abbreviation it fills the engineer's initials.
explanation.definitionFit: A clientele is the body of clients or patrons served by a business, so it means customers collectively.

clue.text: Australian funds prestigious award

blocks.note: first meaning: Australian rhyming slang for cash
second meaning: the statuette given at the Academy Awards

explanation.surface: Australian money paying for a top prize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funds' reads as a verb, sponsoring the award, but it is a noun: money in Australian slang, where Oscar Asche rhymes with cash.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is both Australian slang for money and the familiar name of the Academy Award for film.

clue.text: Important lady found in wreckage of Nazi car

indicators.note: wreckage is something smashed apart, so the letters lie in pieces and must be rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A grand woman discovered in a crashed wartime German staff car.
explanation.walkthrough: The rare Z narrows the shuffle quickly once the fodder is spotted.
explanation.definitionFit: A czarina was the wife of a Russian tsar or an empress, so certainly a woman of high rank.

clue.text: Revolutionary character runs into Lot and Abraham?

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the word is read backwards
going into something means ending up inside it

blocks.note: an air is a manner or demeanour, someone's character
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
a lot is a plot of land, a patch

explanation.surface: A rebel bursting into the Bible story of Lot and Abraham.
explanation.walkthrough: Lot and Abraham look like a biblical pair, but Lot is a piece of ground and only Abraham is the definition; 'Revolutionary' suggests Che, but signals reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Abraham is one of the patriarchs, the founding fathers of Israel in Genesis; the question mark marks him as an example.

clue.text: Enmity encountered in Tehran courthouse

indicators.note: what you encounter in a place is found sitting inside it

blocks.note: runs across the two words

explanation.surface: Hostility met with in an Iranian court.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the city and the building, with no letters added.
explanation.definitionFit: Rancour is bitter, long-lasting resentment, so it is a synonym for hostility.

clue.text: Statesmen arranged financial enquiry

indicators.note: arranging puts things into a new order, so these letters are set out afresh

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Politicians setting up an investigation into money matters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arranged' reads as politicians organising an inquiry, but it shuffles their own letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A means test examines someone's income and assets to decide eligibility for state benefits, an inquiry into finances.

clue.text: Vocal supporter for one who delivers babies?

indicators.note: vocal means spoken, so the word is heard rather than read

blocks.note: a stalk is the stem that holds up a flower or leaf

explanation.surface: A cheerleader for the midwife.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent the stem of a plant and the long-legged bird sound the same; 'Vocal supporter' pretends to be a fan.
explanation.definitionFit: Folklore tells children that the stork brings newborn babies, hence the question mark.

clue.text: People in authority briefly entertaining computing tax

indicators.note: something said briefly is cut short, losing its last letter
a host entertaining guests has them inside the house

blocks.note: 'them' is the colloquial term for those in power, as in us and them
IT is information technology

explanation.surface: Officials taking a short break to host a talk about levies on computers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Them' as in 'us and them' means the authorities; cut short, it wraps the computing abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A tithe was a tenth of produce or income paid to support the church, a kind of tax.

clue.text: Group included in ban on Etonians

indicators.note: something included in a phrase is contained within it

blocks.note: runs across the three words

explanation.surface: A clique caught up in a ban on boys from Eton College.
explanation.walkthrough: Etonians are pupils of Eton, the English private school; the answer spans the end of the first word to the start of the last.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonet is a set of nine, especially nine musicians, so it is a group.

clue.text: Urine's a little vile

blocks.note: number one is the nursery word for a wee, written No. 1 with the numeral as I
some means a small amount

explanation.surface: A remark that urine is slightly disgusting.
explanation.walkthrough: The childish euphemism number one is abbreviated No. 1, and the digit becomes the Roman letter I; the 's is just 'is', joining the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisome means offensive or disgusting, especially in smell, which matches vile.

clue.text: The reverberation effect made on lutes originally?

definitions.text: The reverberation effect made on lutes originally?

indicators.note: originally means at the outset, so each word gives only its opening letter

blocks.clueFragment: The reverberation effect made on lutes originally
blocks.note: first letters of all seven words

explanation.surface: A musician describing the shimmering sound produced on lutes in early music.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: its initials spell the answer, and read normally it describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tremolo is a wavering, trembling effect produced by rapid repetition of a note, as on plucked strings.

clue.text: Three car makers organised test of public opinion

indicators.note: organising sets things into a fresh order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Three motor manufacturers commission a survey of consumers.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the carmakers commission a survey; 'organised' is really the signal for the fourteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Market research gathers consumers' views and preferences by surveys, a way of sampling what the public thinks.
